item.mechanism: Prolonged mechanical milling causes wear of the high-carbon steel milling media (jar and balls), introducing carbon and iron into the powder, which subsequently precipitates as ZrC carbides and Fe contamination during sintering.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) powders and bulks
item.operating_conditions: Mechanical alloying in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill with AISI 52100 steel balls (15 mm diameter) and jar under argon atmosphere; Sintering at 1200 °C in vacuum using graphite dies
item.supporting_observation: Carbide formation detected after 3 h of milling; Fe content increases from undetectable to 1.8 at.% (30 h) and 2.2 at.% (50 h); ZrC fraction increases from 2.0 wt.% (3 h) to 6.8 wt.% (50 h)
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for non-milled powders (0 h) where no carbides are present; contamination is explicitly linked to the use of carbon steel media and graphite dies, not inherent to the alloy chemistry itself
item.alternatives_considered: Oxide formation is also observed but attributed to wear of media and SPS consolidation; the text notes that carbide formation is thermodynamically more favorable than other carbides in this system
quotes: Carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.
Fe's presence is an indicator of powder and bulk contamination during milling due to the use of carbon steel milling media.
It seems that the formation of zirconium carbide is the most thermodynamically favorable in the given system and used conditions.

item.mechanism: Extended milling time induces severe plastic deformation and grain refinement in the powder, which translates to a finer grain size in the sintered bulk, contributing to increased hardness via the Hall–Petch effect.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA bulks sintered from powders milled for 3 to 50 hours
item.operating_conditions: Powders milled for varying times (3, 10, 30, 50 h) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure
item.supporting_observation: Average grain size decreases from 33.8 µm (3 h) to 25.2 µm (50 h); hardness increases from 592.9 HV (3 h) to 675.7 HV (50 h)
item.scope_limits: The text states that milling times beyond 20 h do not induce further phase changes in powders, but grain refinement continues; the mechanism is specific to the powder metallurgy route and not liquid state casting
item.alternatives_considered: Lack of preferential texture is noted as a characteristic of the PM process, distinguishing it from cast materials which may have texture; the mechanism competes with contamination effects which also increase hardness
quotes: Longer milling times used for powder preparation for mechanical alloying produce more refined microstructures in the bulks.
This is a direct consequence of the severe plastic deformation caused by the prolonged mechanical milling, which results in a rise in hardness proportionally with the time of milling.

Increased milling times combined with short sintering times lead to more fine-grained microstructures compared to cast materials, which can importantly contribute to the enhancement of the mechanical properties, such as hardness and strength.

item.mechanism: Oxide formation (specifically TiO2) occurs during sintering due to the wear of milling media and the sintering process itself, even when protective atmospheres are used, leading to oxide dispersion strengthening.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA bulks
item.operating_conditions: Sintering at 1200 °C in vacuum; powders milled for 30 h and 50 h; protective argon atmosphere used during milling
item.supporting_observation: Oxides (TiO2) observed after 30 h of milling; TiO2 crystal structure appears in bulks from 30 h and 50 h milled powders but not in powders or bulks from 3 h/10 h
item.scope_limits: Oxides were not detected in bulks from powders milled for 3 h or 10 h; the mechanism is specific to longer milling times and the SPS consolidation step
item.alternatives_considered: The text suggests that while oxides/carbides are contamination, they can be exploited for oxide dispersed strengthening (ODS) effect
quotes: Oxides were observed after 30 h due to wear of the high-carbon steel milling media and SPS consolidation.
One may exploit the formation of oxides/carbides as a way of exploring the oxide dispersed strengthening (ODS) effect.

item.mechanism: Mechanical alloying drives solid solution formation and phase transformation from elemental powders to a dominant BCC1 solid solution, with secondary phases (HCP, BCC2) dissolving or decreasing as milling time increases.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA powders
item.operating_conditions: Mechanical alloying for 0 to 50 hours in a planetary ball mill under argon atmosphere
item.supporting_observation: After 1 h, four phases (BCC1, BCC2, HCP1, HCP2) exist; after 20 h, a single BCC1 solid solution is achieved; after 10 h, BCC1 reaches almost the whole weight of the alloy
item.scope_limits: The HCP phase observed in powders is not exhibited in the sintered alloys due to fast cooling; the mechanism is specific to the solid-state mechanical alloying process
item.alternatives_considered: CALPHAD predicts HCP_A3 formation below 600 °C, but it was not observed in the bulk due to processing conditions
quotes: Solid solution forming reactions should occur upon the start of the milling process of the mixed powders.
After 20 h of milling, a single BCC1 solid solution is already achieved.
After 10 h of milling, the BCC1 is clearly dominant, reaching almost the whole weight of the alloy.

item.mechanism: The formation of a second BCC phase (BCC2) in the sintered bulk is attributed to spinodal decomposition or a BCC_A2/BCC_B2 relationship, similar to coherent phase relationships found in superalloys.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA bulks (specifically from 10 h and 30 h milled powders)
item.operating_conditions: Sintering at 1200 °C; powders milled for 10 h and 30 h
item.supporting_observation: Bulks from 10 h and 30 h milled powders exhibit two BCC phases (BCC1 and BCC2) with very close lattice parameters; CALPHAD predicts this phase behavior
item.scope_limits: BCC2 is absent in the bulk from 50 h milled powder; the mechanism is not observed in the 3 h bulk; the text notes the second phase might be nano-sized and below EBSD resolution
item.alternatives_considered: The text considers that the BCC2 phase might be a result of spinodal decomposition, referencing similar alloys produced by arc melting
quotes: Two BCC phases were proven to exist in similar alloys in a BCC_A2/BCC_B2 relationship, as a result of spinodal decomposition.
These lattices are very similar to the ones obtained in the present study for both BCC1 and BCC2 phases, indicating that they might have a BCC_A2 and BCC_B2 relationship.
Both BCC phases were predicted by the CALPHAD method using the ThermoCalc software as well, in agreement with the experimental results shown here.

item.mechanism: The sintering process promotes the formation of ZrC carbides from carbon introduced during milling, with the graphite die potentially contributing to further contamination.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA bulks
item.operating_conditions: Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C in vacuum using graphite dies with NB coating
item.supporting_observation: ZrC appeared in all sintered alloys but not in the powders before sintering; ZrC fraction increases with milling time (2.0 wt.% at 3 h to 6.8 wt.% at 50 h)
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is specific to the sintering step; the text notes that the graphite die plays an important role in contamination
item.alternatives_considered: The text suggests that while carbides are contamination, they contribute to strength and wear resistance
quotes: Before sintering, the powders did not present peaks corresponding to the ZrC structure, as opposed to the sintered alloys where ZrC appeared in all cases.
The sintering seems to promote the formation of the cubic structure Fm-3m of ZrC and possibly contributes to further contamination due to the use of graphite dies.
The graphite dies have already been reported to play an important role in the contamination of the sintered bulks by SPS.

item.mechanism: 10 hours of milling provides an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity, refinement, and minimal contamination, balancing the benefits of alloying against the drawbacks of media wear.
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA powders and bulks
item.operating_conditions: Mechanical alloying for 10 hours; subsequent SPS sintering
item.supporting_observation: At 10 h, powders are virtually fully homogeneously alloyed with no significant segregation; contamination (Fe, carbides) is lower than at 30 h or 50 h; hardness is high but not maximal
item.scope_limits: This is an optimization recommendation for this specific alloy and process; longer milling times yield higher hardness but at the cost of increased contamination
item.alternatives_considered: Shorter milling times (3 h) result in lower homogeneity and hardness; longer times (30-50 h) result in excessive contamination
quotes: Ten hours of milling seems sufficient for achieving an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity and refinement, high hardness and minimal contamination.
Milling for 10 h provides the best balance between sufficient microstructural refinement, homogeneity, high hardness and minimal contamination.

item.mechanism: The elastic modulus of the sintered bulk increases slightly with milling time, correlated with the increase in hardness and the presence of dispersed hard phases (carbides/oxides).
item.system: Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA bulks
item.operating_conditions: Sintered bulks from powders milled 3 to 50 h; tested via nanoindentation and ultrasound methods
item.supporting_observation: Elastic modulus increases from 134.7 GPa (3 h) to 138.7 GPa (50 h); a 3% increase in elastic modulus is noted with increasing milling times
item.scope_limits: The increase is described as 'slight'; the mechanism is linked to the microstructural changes (refinement, contamination) rather than a fundamental change in the base BCC phase properties
item.alternatives_considered: The text notes that the elastic modulus from nanoindentation and ultrasound methods show similar results, validating the measurement
quotes: The elastic modulus, as reflected by the Oliver–Pharr method and also by the slope of the unloading part of the nanoindentation curves, shows a slight increase with the increase in hardness, from 134.7 GPa up to 138.7 GPa.
The elastic modulus of the sintered bulks increased by 3% with increasing milling times.
The elastic modulus from both methods shows similar results for this specific time of milling (≈136 GPa).
